The estimation of interaction and quadratic effects in regression models with observed variables is a well-known procedure [@aiken_west_1991; @rimpler_etall_2025]. In that case, an interaction is calculated by the product of certain predictors, whereas a quadratic term involves the product of a predictor with itself. This allows researchers to study, for example, the dependency that one variable may have on the level of another variable. In a structural equation model (SEM) we usually have regressions with latent variables (i.e., latent variable model or structural part; @bollen_model_2019). This creates issues for estimating interaction and quadratic effects because the scores (i.e., the subject-specific values) on the latent variables are, at least at the time of measurement, unobserved [@bollen_latent_2012].

Despite that, the possibility to estimate latent interaction and quadratic terms is important. Indeed, for instance, previous research (with observed variables) suggests that quadratic and interaction effects may "mask" or distort each other when predictors are correlated, which may lead to incorrect conclusions about the nature and direction of effects if not estimated simultaneously [@belzak_interaction_2019; @ganzach_misleading_1997]. Second, researchers in social and behavioral sciences should not have their theoretical models constrained by technical limitations — if theory suggests nonlinear effects exist, appropriate methods should be available to test these hypotheses rigorously. Moreover, SEM explicitly models measurement error in these product terms by partitioning variance into latent constructs and error terms, where this depends on the validity of our measurement model assumptions. This is particularly important because the reliability of a product term is lower than that of its components [@ng_chan_2020]. Thus, estimating interactions with latent variables would provide us with predictors that, in theory, do not contain measurement error. This also has consequences with respect to minimizing bias in the estimates for the regression parameters in the structural model. Adding to that, Marsh et al. (2012, as cited in Cham et al., 2012) highlighted that a latent variable model contributes to higher statistical power, but this may not necessarily hold in general [@Fuller1987].

Multiple methods were proposed in the past years that reflect successive attempts to address specific limitations identified in previous methods [@kenny_judd_1984; @joreskog_yan_1996; @algina_moulder_2001; @klein_moosbrugger_2000; @marsh_etall_2004; @bollen_1995; @wall_amemiya_gapi_2001; @mooijaart_bentler_2010; @mooijaart_satorra_2012; @boker_etall_2023]. However, these approaches differ substantially in their practical accessibility and in the assumptions required for their estimators to maintain desirable properties. For a detailed theoretical-overview of assumptions and expected performance, we refer the reader to @kelava_brandt_2022. To empirically evaluate the performance of those, simulation studies [@marsh_etall_2004, @cham_etall_2012, @brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @lonati_etall_2025] have provided general guidelines and findings with respect to the different approaches when it comes to bias, type I error rate, and power, for instance. 

The initial approach, the so-called Product Indicator (PI) approach [@kenny_judd_1984], was based on constructing product indicators of the nonlinear latent variables by multiplying the indicators of the latent variables included in the interaction or quadratic term. Importantly, early implementations imposed restrictive multiple nonlinear constraints [@joreskog_yan_1996; @kelava_etall_2011]. Subsequent developments relaxed these constraints: the Generalized Appended Product Indicators (GAPI) approach removed normality assumptions for predictor latent variables [@wall_amemiya_gapi_2001], while the Unconstrained Product Indicators (UPI) approach^[The Extended Unconstrained Approach (ExUC) further extended UPI to handle both quadratic and interaction effects [@kelava_brandt_2009].] eliminated parameter constraints entirely [@marsh_etall_2004]. Research has also explored optimal strategies for constructing product indicators and various centering approaches, including mean-centering, residual centering, and double mean centering [@marsh_etall_2004; @schoemann_jorgensen_2021; @kjell_etall_2024]. 

Another relevant class of approaches is the distribution analytic approaches. 

In this article, we highlight the approaches used in our simulation study.

# Existing methods for estimating latent nonlinear effects

## Product Indicator (PI) approaches

The initial approach, the so-called Product Indicator (PI) approach [@kenny_judd_1984], was based on constructing product indicators (hence, the name) of the nonlinear latent variables by multiplying the indicators of the latent variables included in the interaction (or quadratic term). This early implementation imposed several constraints in the model [@joreskog_yan_1996; @kelava_etall_2011; see Appendix in @marsh_etall_2004]. Most of these constraints are connected to the structural specifications on the model. Later on, possible simplifications were proposed and extended. @joreskog_yan_1996 reported that a single indicator for the interaction term was enough instead of all possible pairs. Moreover, the authors argued that the means of the observed variables should be present in the estimation. This was later noted unnecessary if one would mean-center the indicators, and provided to solve convergence issues [@algina_moulder_2001]. @wall_amemiya_gapi_2001 highlighted that the assumption of normally distributed latent variables (i.e., $\eta_x$, referring to the latent predictor variables, which in their notation $\xi$ was used) imposed constraints in the covariance-variance matrix which were not sustainable. This lead to the Generalized Appended Product Indicators (GAPI) approach that did not have the restrictions in the abovementioned matrix (i.e., there was no assumption of normality for the latent variable in the GAPI method), but still involved constraining other parameters as in the constrained procedures. @marsh_etall_2004 showed that the constraints were not necessarily connected to a better estimation. Thus, the authors proposed another approach: Unconstrained Product Indicators (UPI) approach. Building on top of the UPI approach, @kelava_brandt_2009 presented an extension, called Extended Unconstrained Approach (ExUC), to also include models with both quadratic and interaction effects (as initially, most literature only focused on models without quadratic terms).

The literature concerning PI approaches also investigated important aspects with respect to strategies (i.e., all pairs, matched-pairs) for constructing product indicators and mean-centering - which was also later developed further into residual centering and double mean centering [@marsh_etall_2004; @schoemann_jorgensen_2021; @kjell_etall_2024].

## Distribution Analytic (DA) approaches

Another class of methods is the distribution analytic approach. In order to tackle the normality assumption that is violated in the product indicator approaches, the LMS approach was proposed [@klein_moosbrugger_2000]. This method is a full-information ML estimator [@kelava_nonlinear_2014]. Moreover, the distribution analytic methods do not create measurement models for the nonlinear terms as in the product indicator approaches. Another approach within this class is the QML.

The LMS approach is based on approximating the non-normal distribution of the observed indicators by a mixture of normal distributions [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_brandt_2022; @kelava_etall_2011]. Briefly, the vector space of the latent variables is partitioned into two subvectors: one includes the terms involved in the nonlinear effects and the other only linear terms. Hence, given that one subvector takes different values, each with an associated distribution, one is able to use a mixture model to encompass all the different possibilities. This mixture model, in the end, integrates the multivariate distributions, which are weighted accordingly. Indeed, this done with the application of the EM algorithm.

The QML approach is somewhat distinct, but it aims to solve the same issue: nonnormality of the indicators of the dependent latent variable. In fact, this estimator was developed to decrease the computational intensive in comparison to the LMS approach and increase robustness with respect to nonnormal latent predictors. The key idea in QML is replacing the complex nonnormal distribution with a normal approximation that preserves the same mean and variance, allowing standard maximum likelihood techniques to be used. This approach creates difference scores to isolate normally distributed components, conditions out normal parts from the scaling variable, and represents the joint distribution as a product that can be more easily approximated. The result is a more computationally efficient procedure with only a small loss of statistical efficiency compared to LMS.

With respect to the distributional assumptions, the LMS and QML estimators assumes multivariate normality for all latent exogenous variables ($\eta_x$, for instance) as well as for the residual variables (to be clarified; this means really all equations' residuals). In contrast, for the NSEMM, the assumption of normally distributed latent variables is not required. This approach integrates aspects of the abovementioned estimators with semiparametric approaches for the estimation of nonlinear terms.

## Structural-after-Measurement (SAM) approaches

Several SAM approaches were proposed in the literature. @wall_amemiya_2003 proposed the two-stage method of moments (2SMM), which is an errors-in-variables regression where factor scores are estimated in an initial stage and in a second stage those are used in a regression for the structural model. Moreover, Ng and Chan (2020) as well as Cox and Kelcey (2021) also proposed certain procedures for the estimation of interaction terms. 

Recently, Rosseel et al. (2025) proposed a method that is closely related to the 2SMM: the local SAM (LSAM). This approach allows for the estimation of interacion and quadratic terms. 

Several SAM methods have been proposed in the literature for handling latent quadratic and interaction effects. SAM approaches offer a practical alternative to joint estimation methods by separating the estimation of measurement and structural parameters into two sequential steps. The two-stage method of moments (2SMM; Wall & Amemiya, 2000) represents the most general approach, using Bartlett factor scores to construct polynomial terms of arbitrary order and adjusting their crossproducts to correct for measurement error through an errors-in-variables framework. This method provides consistent estimators without assuming normality for factors or measurement errors. However, due to its implementation complexity, no software available. Ng and Chan (2020) proposed a simpler procedure extending the Skrondal and Laake (2001) bias-avoiding approach, using regression factor scores for latent predictors and Bartlett factor scores for latent response variables before applying standard regression to the resulting higher-order terms. While this method exhibits some negative bias with low indicator reliability, it remains computationally straightforward and can accommodate multiple quadratic and interaction terms without specialized software. Cox and Kelcey (2021) extended Croon's (2002) bias-correction method to latent interactions by adjusting the augmented variance-covariance matrix of factor scores, dividing covariances by products of factor score and loading matrices while using the Bohrnstedt-Goldberger formula for interaction variances under normality assumptions. Most recently, Rosseel et al. (2024) introduced the local SAM (LSAM) approach, which uses a mapping matrix to project observed statistics onto the latent space and employs Kronecker products to systematically generate second-order terms with distribution-free approximations for their augmented statistics. The LSAM method can be viewed as a special case of 2SMM restricted to second-order terms but with explicit matrix formulas that facilitate software implementation. All four methods successfully address the scalability limitations of joint estimation approaches, enabling practical estimation of models with numerous nonlinear terms while maintaining computational feasibility.

## Other approaches

In the previous paragraphs we described some of the well-known approaches. There are, however, many others, which are not investigated in this article and therefore are briefly described. @bollen_1995 introduced the model-implied instrumental variables two-stage least-squares (MIIV-2SLS) approach. @mooijaart_bentler_2010 proposed a methods-of-moments (MM) approach. More recently, a Products of Variables Model (PoV) approach was developed @boker_etall_2023. There are also other nonparametric approaches.

## This article

The primary objective of this article is to further investigate the recently proposed SAM method: the LSAM [@rosseel_etall_2025] [^2]. In @rosseel_etall_2025, a small simulation study was conducted to evaluate the LSAM approach. The primary scope was limited to examining the bias and variability of the point estimates involved in the nonlinear terms. This paper aims to further extend it by analyzing standard errors, coverage, type I error rate, and power.

[^2]: This approach is closely connected to the more general two-stage method of moments (2SMM) [@wall_amemiya_2000; @wall_amemiya_2003].  As noted in @rosseel_etall_2025, and opposed to the 2SMM, the LSAM does not require the structural part to be recursive, nor needs to distinguish in advance between endogenous and exogenous variables. Moreover, it is not needed to center the latent predictors involved in the nonlinear effects. Importantly, both do not require the latent predictors to follow a normal distribution. 

To study the performance of the LSAM, we will compare it with some of the more widely used and available methods in one simulation study: Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS), Unconstrained Product Indicator with double-mean centering (DBLCENT), and the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood (QML) approach. This simulation study will investigate standard errors, bias, coverage, type I error rate, and power. In a second simulation study will assess the "scalibility" of the LSAM approach. The LMS, QML, and UCA are known to scale given the increase of nonlinear effects (i.e., interaction and quadratic terms) in the model. The LSAM, on the other hand, should not be affected by this. 

This paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we provide a brief overview of the statistical models under evaluation approaches, together with the assumptions. We then present the simulation design, computational details, and performance measures. Following that, we report the results of our simulation studies. The last section concludes with a discussion that integrates our findings with the results from previous simulation studies.
